items.title: Sub-Part 21: The Restless Mind, and What Actually Tames It

items.zh: 難調伏、輕躁，淪墜於諸欲；善調伏其心，心調引安樂。
items.en: Hard to tame, restless, forever sinking into desires — but a mind well tamed, once tamed, brings genuine ease.

items.zh: 此頌所明，謂宣說心、若意、若識，長夜愛樂憒鬧雜處，於憒鬧處難得遠離、難可調伏。雖強安處無間修習諸善法中，而不一向能住離貪、離瞋、離癡，亦不一向能住策舉、無掉、寂靜；然復疾疾還生有貪、有瞋、有癡、下劣、掉舉及不寂靜。雖強安處內寂止中，長夜愛樂色聲香味觸故，於五欲境馳趣淪沒。諸聖弟子，於如是等樂著雜染能生苦心，終不縱其令自在轉，亦不隨順；數數思擇成辦遠離，恒修善法心一境性。彼由如是正定心故，能如實知；如實知故，能起厭患；由厭患故，能得離染；由離染故，能得解脫。彼既如是善調伏心盡苦因故，於現法中得安樂住，當來眾苦亦得永盡。復次，今當略辨上所說義。謂薄伽梵此中略示，能不隨順長夜流轉左道之心，及不隨順所得勝利。當知是名此中略義。
items.en: This verse explains that the mind, also called mentation or consciousness, has for a long time delighted in crowds and bustle, and in the midst of bustle it is hard to keep it apart and hard to tame. Even if it is forcibly settled in the uninterrupted cultivation of wholesome qualities, it cannot invariably abide free of greed, free of anger and free of delusion, nor can it invariably abide roused, without restlessness and at peace; very quickly it again becomes greedy, angry, deluded, sluggish, restless and not at peace. Even if it is forcibly settled in inner calm, because it has for a long time delighted in forms, sounds, smells, tastes and tangibles, it runs towards and sinks into the objects of the five sense pleasures. The noble disciples never let such a mind, which delights in defilement and can give rise to suffering, run free, nor do they go along with it; again and again they reflect, bring about seclusion, and constantly cultivate wholesome qualities and one-pointedness of mind. Through such a rightly concentrated mind they are able to know as it really is; because they know as it really is, they are able to give rise to disenchantment; through disenchantment they are able to become free of desire; through freedom from desire they are able to attain liberation. Because they have thus tamed the mind well and exhausted the causes of suffering, they gain a happy abiding here and now, and future sufferings are also exhausted for ever. Further, the meaning of what was said above will now be briefly set out. In this verse the Blessed One briefly shows not going along with the mind that has for a long time drifted along the wrong path, and the benefit gained by not going along with it. It should be understood that this is the summary meaning here.

items.title: Sub-Part 22: Knowing When to Calm, When to Rouse, When to Simply Let Be

items.zh: 於心相善知，能餐遠離味、靜慮、常委、念、受無染喜樂。
items.en: Knowing well the mind's own signs, one savours the taste of seclusion; through meditation, mindfulness constant and thorough, one experiences the ease freed from joy and the untainted ease.

items.zh: 此頌所明，謂如有一，有學見迹，能善了知止、舉、捨相。由此因緣，得四功德。謂心住一緣，遠離麁重，能善受用身心安樂；是初功德。又淨定心盡所修故、如所修故，能正審慮諸法道理，獲得內法毘鉢舍那；是第二功德。彼由如是清淨止觀為依止故，於所修習菩提分法，勇猛無間，能常修習、能委修習，無懈無憚；是第三功德。彼由如是無懈憚心，獲得第一正念正知心善解脫，又能受用解脫喜樂及無染樂，於現法中得安樂住；是第四功德。復次，今當略辨上所說義。謂薄伽梵此中略示，於相善巧四種功德。謂奢摩他所作、毘鉢舍那所作、無懈憚所作、到究竟所作。當知是名此中略義。
items.en: This verse explains the following. Someone in training who has seen the track [of the truths] is able to understand well the signs of calm, of exertion and of equanimity. For this reason they gain four virtues. The mind abides on a single object, free of coarseness, and is able to enjoy well the ease of body and mind; this is the first virtue. Again, because the purified concentrated mind has been cultivated to its full extent and in the proper way, they are able rightly to examine and consider the principles of phenomena, and gain insight into inner phenomena; this is the second virtue. Relying on such pure calm and insight, they cultivate the factors of awakening with vigour and without interruption; they are able to cultivate them constantly and thoroughly, without laxity and without weariness; this is the third virtue. Through such a mind without laxity or weariness, they gain foremost right mindfulness and right awareness, their mind is well liberated, and they are also able to enjoy the joy of liberation and untainted happiness, gaining a happy abiding here and now; this is the fourth virtue. Further, the meaning of what was said above will now be briefly set out. In this verse the Blessed One briefly shows four kinds of virtue that come from skill in the signs: what calm (śamatha) accomplishes, what insight (vipaśyanā) accomplishes, what freedom from laxity and weariness accomplishes, and what reaching the ultimate accomplishes. It should be understood that this is the summary meaning here.

items.title: Sub-Part 23: What a Genuine Monk Actually Looks Like

items.zh: 無工巧活、輕自己、樂勝、諸根、盡解脫。無家、無所、無悕望、斷欲、獨行真苾芻。
items.en: No contrived livelihood, holding oneself lightly, delighting in what is excellent, the roots exhausted, and liberated — homeless, possessing nothing, hoping for nothing, desire cut off, walking alone: such is the genuine monk.

items.zh: 此頌所明，謂成就五支，永斷五支，當知得名真實苾芻。何等為五？謂不依止矯設方便邪活命法，亦不恃賴有勢之家，亦不修治名稱族望，亦不詐受諸佛所說、聖弟子說；猶如依止工巧處所，非法悕求衣服飲食。是名初支。又復減省器物眾具，善棄珍財，衣僅蔽身，食纔充腹，知足歡喜；凡所遊行，必持衣鉢。是第二支。又悕慕沙門、愛樂沙門，悕慕學處、愛樂學處；命難因緣，尚不違越所學禁戒，何況少小利養因緣。是第三支。又彼如是正修方便，淨命喜足，愛樂學處，於諸聖諦未現觀者，能入現觀，得清淨見；或時失念，暫爾發生惡不善尋，引起貪欲、瞋恚、愚癡，遲緩忘念，速復除遣。是第四支。又彼修習如先得道，於諸結、縛、一切隨眠、隨煩惱、纏，心得解脫。是第五支。如是名為成就五支。云何復名永斷五支？謂阿羅漢苾芻，於五處所不復能犯。所謂不能捨所學處，而復退還。又復不能有所貯積，執為己有而受用之，亦不受用諸欲境界。又復不能為財、為命，知而妄語。又復不能棄捨諸欲，行不與取。亦不復能永離貪欲，獨住獨行，而更習近非梵行法，兩兩交會。或計自作而招苦樂，或計他作、或自他作、或非自作亦非他作，不由因生而招苦樂。如是名為五支永斷。
items.en: This verse explains that one who possesses five factors and has cut off five factors for ever should be understood to be called a genuine monk. What are the five? They do not rely on the wrong livelihood of contrived schemes; they do not depend on powerful families; they do not cultivate fame and reputation for their family line; and they do not falsely take up what was taught by the buddhas and by the noble disciples, using it like a place of crafts to seek clothing and food contrary to the Dharma. This is called the first factor. Again, they reduce their belongings and provisions, give up precious wealth well, wear clothing just enough to cover the body and eat food just enough to fill the belly, and are content and glad; wherever they wander, they always carry their robes and bowl. This is the second factor. Again, they long for the ascetic life and love the ascetic life, long for the points of training and love the points of training; even when their life is in danger they would not transgress the prohibitions they have undertaken to train in, still less for the sake of small gains and honours. This is the third factor. Again, practising right effort in this way, with pure livelihood and contentment, loving the points of training, they are able to enter direct realisation of the noble truths that they have not yet directly realised, and obtain pure vision; and if at times, through loss of mindfulness, bad and unwholesome thoughts briefly arise and stir up greed, anger or delusion, then, though slow to notice through forgetfulness, they quickly remove them again. This is the fourth factor. Again, by cultivating the path previously attained, their mind is liberated from all fetters, bonds, all latent tendencies, secondary afflictions and entanglements. This is the fifth factor. This is called possessing five factors. And how is one called one who has cut off five factors for ever? An arhat monk can no longer transgress in five respects. They cannot give up the points of training and turn back. Again, they cannot store anything up, treating it as their own and using it, nor do they enjoy the objects of sense pleasure. Again, they cannot knowingly tell a lie for the sake of wealth or for the sake of life. Again, having given up sense pleasures, they cannot take what is not given. Nor, being for ever free of sensual greed and dwelling and walking alone, can they again indulge in what is not the holy life, the coupling of two together; or hold that pleasure and pain are brought about by oneself, or by another, or by both oneself and another, or neither by oneself nor by another but arising without a cause. This is called having cut off five factors for ever.

blocks.text: Three verses on taming the mind and on the genuine renunciant. The explanations are **missing from Ru-Yi's translation**; the English column gives our own translation, and the commentary summarises them.
"Hard to tame, restless, forever sinking into desires; but a mind well tamed brings genuine ease." Master Cháng Bǎi: like a monkey, never still for a moment.

The prose: mind (心、意、識) has delighted in noise and crowds through the long night, and finds solitude hard. Even when made to practise, it does not stay free of greed, hatred, and delusion, or balanced, but quickly falls back into them, and even in inner calm runs after sense objects. The noble disciple does not let such a mind have its way, keeps choosing solitude and one-pointedness, and so knows as it is; from knowing, disenchantment; from disenchantment, dispassion; from dispassion, liberation. Such a mind is at ease now, and future suffering ends.
"Knowing well the mind's signs, one savours seclusion; meditating with constant, thorough mindfulness, one experiences untainted joy and ease."

The prose: a trainee who knows the signs of **calming** (止), **rousing** (舉), and **equanimity** (捨), knowing when the mind needs each, gains four benefits: one-pointedness and ease of body and mind (the work of calm); clear insight into the Dharma (the work of insight); tireless practice of the factors of awakening, "constant and thorough" (Master Cháng Bǎi: without interruption, and with care); and the joy of liberation here and now.

"No contrived livelihood, holding oneself lightly, delighting in what is excellent, the roots exhausted, liberated; homeless, possessing nothing, hoping for nothing, desire cut off": such a one is a true monk.

The prose: a true monk **possesses five factors**: no wrong livelihood, flattery, or dependence on powerful families; few possessions, robes just to cover the body, food just to fill the stomach (Master Cháng Bǎi: "holding oneself lightly" means not clinging to a self, not looking down on oneself); love of the training, not breaking a rule even at risk of life; seeing the truths, and quickly dismissing any lapse of mindfulness; and liberation from all fetters.

And the arhat **has abandoned five things**: he cannot give up the training; cannot hoard; cannot knowingly lie; cannot steal; cannot engage in sexual conduct. Nor does he hold that pleasure and pain are made by oneself, by another, by both, or by neither.

quiz.q: What does the twenty-first verse say of the mind?
options: the mind is pure and needs no taming
hard to tame, restless, sinking into desires; a mind well tamed brings ease
the mind is a bright moon
quiz.why: "Hard to tame, restless, forever sinking into desires — but a mind well tamed, once tamed, brings genuine ease." Master Cháng Bǎi: the ordinary person's mind is hard to tame and restless, like a monkey never still for a moment.

quiz.q: What image does Master Cháng Bǎi use for "restless"?
options: a monkey, never still for a moment
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the ordinary person's mind, thought, and consciousness are hard to tame and restless, like a monkey that is not still for a moment.

quiz.q: According to the twenty-second verse, what does one who knows the mind's signs well attain?
options: savours the taste of seclusion; through meditation with constant thorough mindfulness, experiences untainted joy and ease
quiz.why: "Knowing well the mind's own signs, one savours the taste of seclusion; through meditation, mindfulness constant and thorough, one experiences joy and ease untainted." Master Cháng Bǎi: the sign of equanimity is like smoothly entering a highway — the mind runs without effort.

quiz.q: How do the two masters explain 常 and 委 in "mindfulness constant and thorough"?
options: 常 is without interruption; 委 is earnest and careful, practising subtly and thoroughly
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: practising the four foundations of mindfulness without interruption is "constant"; practising them earnestly and carefully is "thorough." Venerable Miào Jìng: 常 means unbroken diligence; 委 means practising subtly and comprehensively, not coarsely.

quiz.q: The note says "desire cut off" means no sexual activity. How do the masters, following the treatise, assign "desire cut off" and "walking alone"?
options: desire cut off means not taking what is not given (no stealing); walking alone means no unchaste conduct — the note mismatches them
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the fourth is never stealing; the fifth is never having sexual desire. Venerable Miào Jìng: an arhat would not give up many desires and then go steal others' things. The note treats "desire cut off" as celibacy and omits not stealing.

quiz.q: Does "holding oneself lightly" mean looking down on oneself? How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain it?
options: not self-contempt but not clinging to self — with the wisdom of non-self, content with getting by
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "lightly" does not mean looking down on oneself, but not clinging to a self — having the wisdom of non-self, content as long as life gets by.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain "homeless"?
options: "home" is affliction; homeless means the arhat never returns to lay life
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: first, homeless — "home" is affliction; homeless means the arhat will not return to lay life. Venerable Miào Jìng likewise says that leaving the household is really relinquishing desire.
